metadata.title: An Inertial Tseng's Type Proximal Algorithm for Nonsmooth and Nonconvex Optimization Problems

items.name: Generalized subdifferential and critical points
items.statement:
The domain of the function $f: \mathbb{R}^m \to ] - \infty, +\infty]$ is defined by $\operatorname{dom} f := \{x \in \mathbb{R}^m : f(x) < +\infty\}$ . We say that $f$ is proper if $\operatorname{dom} f \neq \emptyset$ . Further we recall some generalized subdifferential notions and the basic properties which are needed in the paper, see [30,31]. Let $f: \mathbb{R}^m \to ] - \infty, +\infty]$ be a proper and lower semicontinuous function. If $x \in \operatorname{dom} f$ , we consider the Fréchet (viscosity) subdifferential of $f$ at $x$ as the set

$$
\hat {\partial} f (x) := \left\{v \in \mathbb {R} ^ {m}: \operatorname * {l i m i n f} _ {y \to x} \frac {f (y) - f (x) - \langle v , y - x \rangle}{\| y - x \|} \geq 0 \right\}.
$$

For $x \notin \text{dom } f$ we set $\hat{\partial} f(x) := \emptyset$ . The limiting (Mordukhovich) subdifferential is defined at a point $x \in \text{dom } f$ by

$$
\partial f (x) = \{v \in \mathbb {R} ^ {m}: \exists x _ {n} \to x, f (x _ {n}) \to f (x) \text {and} \exists v _ {n} \in \hat {\partial} f (x _ {n}), v _ {n} \to v \text {as} n \to + \infty \},
$$

while for $x \notin dom f$ , one takes $\partial f(x) := \emptyset$ .

Notice that in case $f$ is convex, these notions coincide with the convex subdifferential, which means that $\hat{\partial} f(x) = \partial f(x) = \{v \in \mathbb{R}^m : f(y) \geq f(x) + \langle v, y - x \rangle \forall y \in \mathbb{R}^m\}$ for all $x \in \operatorname{dom} f$ .

Notice the inclusion $\hat{\partial}f(x)\subseteq\partial f(x)$ for each $x\in R^{m}$ . We will use the following closedness criteria concerning the graph of the limiting subdifferential: if $(x_{n})_{n\in\mathbb{N}}$ and $(v_{n})_{n\in\mathbb{N}}$ are sequences in $R^{m}$ such that $v_{n}\in\partial f(x_{n})$ for all $n\in N$ , $(x_{n},v_{n})\to(x,v)$ and $f(x_{n})\to f(x)$ as $n\to+\infty$ , then $v\in\partial f(x)$ .

The Fermat rule reads in this nonsmooth setting as: if $x \in \mathbb{R}^m$ is a local minimizer of $f$ , then $0 \in \partial f(x)$ . Notice that in case $f$ is continuously differentiable at $x \in \mathbb{R}^m$ we have $\partial f(x) = \{\nabla f(x)\}$ . Let us denote by

$$
\operatorname{crit} (f) := \{x \in \mathbb {R} ^ {m}: 0 \in \partial f (x) \}
$$

the set of (limiting)-critical points of $f$ . Let us mention also the following subdifferential rule: if $f: \mathbb{R}^m \to ] - \infty, +\infty]$ is proper and lower semicontinuous and $h: \mathbb{R}^m \to \mathbb{R}$ is a continuously differentiable function, then $\partial(f + h)(x) = \partial f(x) + \nabla h(x)$ for all $x \in \mathbb{R}^m$ .

items.name: Definition 2.1 (Kurdyka-Lojasiewicz property)
items.statement:
We turn now our attention to functions satisfying the Kurdyka–Lojasiewicz property. This class of functions will play a crucial role in the convergence results of the proposed algorithm. For $\eta\in]0,+\infty]$ , we denote by $\Theta_{\eta}$ the class of concave and continuous functions $\varphi:[0,\eta[\to[0,+\infty[$ such that $\varphi(0)=0,\varphi$ is continuously differentiable on ]0, $\eta[$ , continuous at 0 and $\varphi'(s)>0$ for all $s\in]0,\eta[$ . In the following definition (see [18,20]), we use also the distance function to a set, defined for $A\subseteq R^{m}$ as $\text{dist}(x,A):=\inf_{y\in A}\|x-y\|$ for all $x\in R^{m}$ .

Definition 2.1 (Kurdyka–Łojasiewicz property) Let $f : \mathbb{R}^{m} \to ] - \infty, +\infty]$ be a proper and lower semicontinuous function. We say that $f$ satisfies the Kurdyka–Łojasiewicz (KL) property at $\overline{x} \in \text{dom } \partial f := \{x \in \mathbb{R}^{m} : \partial f(x) \neq \emptyset\}$ if there exists $\eta \in ]0, +\infty]$ , a neighborhood $U$ of $\overline{x}$ and a function $\varphi \in \Theta_{\eta}$ such that for all $x$ in the intersection

$$
U \cap \{x \in \mathbb {R} ^ {m}: f (\overline {{x}}) <   f (x) <   f (\overline {{x}}) + \eta \}
$$

the following inequality holds

$$
\varphi^ {\prime} (f (x) - f (\overline {{x}})) \mathrm{dist} (0, \partial f (x)) \geq 1.
$$

If $f$ satisfies the KL property at each point in dom $\partial f$ , then $f$ is called a KL function.

items.name: Lemma 2.1
items.statement:
Lemma 2.1 Let $\Omega \subseteq \mathbb{R}^m$ be a compact set and let $f: \mathbb{R}^m \to ]-\infty, +\infty]$ be a proper and lower semicontinuous function. Assume that $f$ is constant on $\Omega$ and $f$ satisfies the KL property at each point of $\Omega$ . Then there exist $\varepsilon, \eta > 0$ and $\varphi \in \Theta_\eta$ such that for all $\overline{x} \in \Omega$ and for all $x$ in the intersection

$$
\{x \in \mathbb {R} ^ {m}: d i s t (x, \Omega) <   \varepsilon \} \cap \{x \in \mathbb {R} ^ {m}: f (\overline {{x}}) <   f (x) <   f (\overline {{x}}) + \eta \} \tag {1}
$$

the following inequality holds

$$
\varphi^ {\prime} (f (x) - f (\overline {{x}})) d i s t (0, \partial f (x)) \geq 1. \tag {2}
$$
items.proof: Cited from: Bolte, J., Sabach, S., Teboulle, M.: Proximal alternating linearized minimization for nonconvex and nonsmooth problems. Math. Program. Ser. A 146(1-2), 459-494 (2014), Lemma 6; the paper cites this as [20, Lemma 6].

items.name: Lemma 2.2
items.statement: Lemma 2.2 Let $(a_{n})_{n\in \mathbb{N}}$ and $(b_{n})_{n\in \mathbb{N}}$ be real sequences such that $b_{n}\geq 0$ for all $n\in \mathbb{N}$ , $(a_{n})_{n\in \mathbb{N}}$ is bounded below and $a_{n + 1} + b_n\leq a_n$ for all $n\in \mathbb{N}$ . Then, $(a_{n})_{n\in \mathbb{N}}$ is a monotonically decreasing and convergent sequence and $\sum_{n\in \mathbb{N}}b_n < +\infty$ .
items.proof: Cited from: Bauschke, H.H., Combettes, P.L.: Convex Analysis and Monotone Operator Theory in Hilbert Spaces. CMS Books in Mathematics. Springer, New York (2011), cited as a standard Fejer monotonicity convergence result before Lemma 2.2.

items.name: Lemma 2.3
items.statement: Lemma 2.3 Let $(\xi_n)_{n\in \mathbb{N}}$ and $(\varepsilon_n)_{n\in \mathbb{N}}$ be sequences in $[0, +\infty[$ such that $\sum_{n\in \mathbb{N}}\varepsilon_n < +\infty$ and $\xi_{n + 1}\leq a\xi_n + b\xi_{n - 1} + \varepsilon_n$ for all $n\geq 1$ , where $a\in \mathbb{R}$ , $b\geq 0$ and $a + b < 1$ . Then $\sum_{n\in \mathbb{N}}\xi_n < +\infty$ .
items.proof: Proof Fix $k \geq 1$ a positive integer. Summing up the inequality from the hypotheses for $n = 1, \ldots, k$ , we obtain $\sum_{n=0}^{k} \xi_{n} + \xi_{k+1} - \xi_{0} - \xi_{1} \leq a \sum_{n=0}^{k} \xi_{n} + b \sum_{n=0}^{k} \xi_{n} - a \xi_{0} - b \xi_{k} + \sum_{n=1}^{k} \varepsilon_{n}$ . Since $\xi_{n} \geq 0$ for all $n \in N$ and $b \geq 0$ , we get $(1 - a - b) \sum_{n=0}^{k} \xi_{n} \leq (1 - a) \xi_{0} + \xi_{1} + \sum_{n=1}^{k} \varepsilon_{n}$ and the conclusion follows. [Indeed, since $1-a-b>0$ and $\sum_n\varepsilon_n<+\infty$, the right-hand side is bounded independently of $k$; hence the increasing partial sums $\sum_{n=0}^k\xi_n$ are uniformly bounded, so $\sum_{n\in\mathbb N}\xi_n<+\infty$.] ☐

items.name: Lipschitz continuous gradient
Problem 3.1
items.statement:
Problem 3.1 Let $m \geq 1$ by a positive integer, $f : \mathbb{R}^m \to -\infty, +\infty]$ be a proper, lower semicontinuous function which is bounded from below and $h : \mathbb{R}^m \to \mathbb{R}$ a Fréchet differentiable function such that $\nabla h$ is $L_{\nabla h}$ -Lipschitz continuous with $L_{\nabla h} \geq 0$ . We aim to solve the optimization problem

$$
(P) \inf _ {x \in \mathbb {R} ^ {m}} [ f (x) + h (x) ] \tag {3}
$$

items.name: Lemma 3.1
items.statement:
Lemma 3.1 Let $h: \mathbb{R}^m \to \mathbb{R}$ be a Fréchet differentiable function with $L_{\nabla h}$ -Lipschitz continuous gradient. Then, we have

$$
h (y) \leq h (x) + \langle \nabla h (x), y - x \rangle + \frac {L _ {\nabla h}}{2} \| y - x \| ^ {2} \forall (x, y) \in \mathbb {R} ^ {m} \times \mathbb {R} ^ {m}.
items.proof: Cited from: Nesterov, Y.: Introductory Lectures on Convex Optimization: A Basic Course. Kluwer Academic, Dordrecht (2004), Lemma 1.2.3, cited immediately before Lemma 3.1.

items.name: Strong convexity with parameter sigma
items.statement: A function $u:\mathbb{R}^m\to\mathbb{R}$ is $\sigma$-strongly convex with parameter $\sigma>0$ if $u-\frac{\sigma}{2}\|\cdot\|^2$ is convex.

items.name: Coercive extended-real-valued function
items.statement: A function $g:\mathbb{R}^m\to\overline{\mathbb{R}}$ is coercive if $\lim_{\|x\|\to+\infty} g(x)=+\infty$, equivalently for every real $c$ the lower level set $\{x:g(x)\le c\}$ is bounded in the finite-dimensional setting used in the paper.

items.name: Argmin set
items.statement: For an extended-real-valued function $G:\mathbb{R}^m\to\overline{\mathbb{R}}$, $\operatorname{argmin}_{x\in\mathbb{R}^m}G(x):=\{p\in\mathbb{R}^m: G(p)=\inf_{x\in\mathbb{R}^m}G(x)\}$.

items.name: Cluster point set of a sequence
items.statement: For a sequence $(z_n)_{n\ge 1}$ in a metric space, $\omega((z_n)_{n\ge 1})$ denotes the set of cluster points, i.e. the set of all $z$ for which there exists a subsequence $(z_{n_k})_{k\in\mathbb{N}}$ with $z_{n_k}\to z$ as $k\to+\infty$.

items.name: Semi-algebraic function
items.statement: A function $g:\mathbb{R}^m\to\overline{\mathbb{R}}$ is semi-algebraic if its graph (equivalently, for extended-real-valued optimization, its epigraph) is a finite union of sets described by finitely many polynomial equalities and strict inequalities.

items.name: Bregman distance generated by u
items.statement: For a differentiable function $u:\mathbb{R}^m\to\mathbb{R}$, the Bregman distance generated by $u$ is $D_u(x,y)=u(x)-u(y)-\langle\nabla u(y),x-y\rangle$ for $x,y\in\mathbb{R}^m$.

items.name: Bregman distance quadratic bounds
items.proof: Cited from: Bauschke, H.H., Combettes, P.L.: Convex Analysis and Monotone Operator Theory in Hilbert Spaces. CMS Books in Mathematics. Springer, New York (2011), referenced in the paper before formula (5).

items.name: Algorithm 3.1
items.statement:
Algorithm 3.1 Choose $x_0, x_1 \in \mathbb{R}^m$ , $\underline{\lambda}, \overline{\lambda} > 0$ , $\alpha \geq 0$ and the sequences $(\lambda_n)_{n \geq 1}$ , $(\alpha_n)_{n \geq 1}$ fulfilling

$$
0 \leq \alpha_ {n} \leq \alpha \forall n \geq 1
$$

and

$$
0 <   \underline {{\lambda}} \leq \lambda_ {n} \leq \overline {{\lambda}} \forall n \geq 1.
$$

Consider the iterative scheme

$$
(\forall n \geq 1) \left\{ \begin{array}{l} p _ {n} \in \underset {x \in \mathbb {R} ^ {m}} {\operatorname{argmin}} \left[ f (x) + \frac {1}{\lambda_ {n}} D _ {u} (x, x _ {n}) + \langle x, \nabla h (x _ {n}) \rangle + \frac {\alpha_ {n}}{\lambda_ {n}} \langle x, x _ {n - 1} - x _ {n} \rangle \right] \\ x _ {n + 1} = p _ {n} + \lambda_ {n} [ \nabla h (x _ {n}) - \nabla h (p _ {n}) ]. \end{array} \right. \tag {4}
$$

Here,

$$
D _ {u}: \mathbb {R} ^ {m} \times \mathbb {R} ^ {m} \to \mathbb {R}, D _ {u} (x, y) = u (x) - u (y) - \langle \nabla u (y), x - y \rangle ,
$$

denotes the Bregman distance of a function $u: \mathbb{R}^m \to \mathbb{R}$ assumed to be $\sigma$ -strongly convex with parameter $\sigma > 0$ (that is $u - \frac{\sigma}{2} \| \cdot \|^2$ is a convex function), differentiable and such that $\nabla u$ is $L_{\nabla u}$ -Lipschitz continuous with $L_{\nabla u} > 0$ .

Notice that the properties of the function $u$ guarantees the following inequality (see for example [1])

$$
\frac {\sigma}{2} \| x - y \| ^ {2} \leq D _ {u} (x, y) \leq \frac {L _ {\nabla u}}{2} \| x - y \| ^ {2} \forall (x, y) \in \mathbb {R} ^ {m} \times \mathbb {R} ^ {m}. \tag {5}
$$

items.name: Lemma 3.2
items.statement:
Lemma 3.2 In the setting of Problem 3.1, consider the sequences generated by Algorithm 3.1. Then for every $\nu$ , $\mu > 0$ the following inequality holds

$$
(f + h) (p _ {n}) + M _ {1} \| x _ {n} - p _ {n} \| ^ {2} \leq (f + h) (p _ {n - 1}) + M _ {2} \| x _ {n - 1} - p _ {n - 1} \| ^ {2} \forall n \geq 2, \tag {9}
$$

where

$$
M _ {1} := \frac {\sigma}{2 \overline {{\lambda}}} - L _ {\nabla h} - \nu - \frac {\alpha}{\underline {{\lambda}}} \mu \tag {10}
$$

and

$$
M _ {2} := \bar {\lambda} ^ {2} L _ {\nabla h} ^ {2} \left(\frac {L _ {\nabla h} ^ {2}}{2 \nu} + \nu + L _ {\nabla h} + \frac {L _ {\nabla u}}{2 \underline {{\lambda}}}\right) + \frac {\alpha}{\underline {{\lambda}}} \left(\mu \bar {\lambda} ^ {2} L _ {\nabla h} ^ {2} + \frac {(1 + \bar {\lambda} L _ {\nabla h}) ^ {2}}{2 \mu}\right). \tag {11}
items.proof:
Proof Let us chose $\nu, \mu > 0$ arbitrary and fix $n \geq 2$ . The rule given in (4) yields the inequality

$$
\begin{array}{l} f (p _ {n}) + \frac {1}{\lambda_ {n}} D _ {u} (p _ {n}, x _ {n}) + \langle p _ {n}, \nabla h (x _ {n}) \rangle + \frac {\alpha_ {n}}{\lambda_ {n}} \langle p _ {n}, x _ {n - 1} - x _ {n} \rangle \\ \leq f (p _ {n - 1}) + \frac {1}{\lambda_ {n}} D _ {u} (p _ {n - 1}, x _ {n}) + \langle p _ {n - 1}, \nabla h (x _ {n}) \rangle + \frac {\alpha_ {n}}{\lambda_ {n}} \left\langle p _ {n - 1}, x _ {n - 1} - x _ {n} \right\rangle , \\ \end{array}
$$

which combined with (5) and [Use the minimizer inequality for $p_n$ with competitor $p_{n-1}$, then substitute the lower bound $D_u(p_n,x_n)\ge(\sigma/2)\|p_n-x_n\|^2$ on the left and the upper bound $D_u(p_{n-1},x_n)\le(L_{\nabla u}/2)\|p_{n-1}-x_n\|^2$ on the right.]

$$
h (p _ {n}) \leq h (p _ {n - 1}) + \langle \nabla h (p _ {n - 1}), p _ {n} - p _ {n - 1} \rangle + \frac {L _ {\nabla h}}{2} \| p _ {n} - p _ {n - 1} \| ^ {2}
$$

gives

$$
\begin{array}{l} (f + h) (p _ {n}) + \frac {\sigma}{2 \lambda_ {n}} \| p _ {n} - x _ {n} \| ^ {2} \leq (f + h) (p _ {n - 1}) + \frac {L _ {\nabla u}}{2 \lambda_ {n}} \| x _ {n} - p _ {n - 1} \| ^ {2} \\ + \frac {L _ {\nabla h}}{2} \| p _ {n} - p _ {n - 1} \| ^ {2} \\ + \langle \nabla h (p _ {n - 1}) - \nabla h (x _ {n}), p _ {n} - p _ {n - 1} \rangle \\ + \frac {\alpha_ {n}}{\lambda_ {n}} \left\langle p _ {n} - p _ {n - 1}, x _ {n} - x _ {n - 1} \right\rangle . \tag {12} \\ \end{array}
$$

According to (4) we have [From $x_n=p_{n-1}+\lambda_{n-1}(\nabla h(x_{n-1})-\nabla h(p_{n-1}))$, subtract $p_{n-1}$ and apply the Lipschitz continuity of $\nabla h$; the displayed norm should be read with $\nabla h$, not $h$, inside the norm.]

$$
\| x _ {n} - p _ {n - 1} \| = \lambda_ {n - 1} \| h (x _ {n - 1}) - h (p _ {n - 1}) \| \leq \lambda_ {n - 1} L _ {\nabla h} \| x _ {n - 1} - p _ {n - 1} \| \tag {13}
$$

and, from here,

$$
\| x _ {n} - x _ {n - 1} \| \leq (1 + \lambda_ {n - 1} L _ {\nabla h}) \| x _ {n - 1} - p _ {n - 1} \| \tag {14}
$$

and

$$
\| p _ {n} - p _ {n - 1} \| ^ {2} \leq 2 (\| x _ {n} - p _ {n} \| ^ {2} + \lambda_ {n - 1} ^ {2} L _ {\nabla h} ^ {2} \| x _ {n - 1} - p _ {n - 1} \| ^ {2}). \tag {15}
$$

Moreover, we have

$$
\langle \nabla h (p _ {n - 1}) - \nabla h (x _ {n}), p _ {n} - p _ {n - 1} \rangle \leq \frac {\nu}{2} \| p _ {n} - p _ {n - 1} \| ^ {2} + \frac {L _ {\nabla h} ^ {2}}{2 \nu} \| x _ {n} - p _ {n - 1} \| ^ {2} \tag {16}
$$

and

$$
\langle p _ {n} - p _ {n - 1}, x _ {n} - x _ {n - 1} \rangle \leq \frac {\mu}{2} \| p _ {n} - p _ {n - 1} \| ^ {2} + \frac {1}{2 \mu} \| x _ {n} - x _ {n - 1} \| ^ {2}. \tag {17}
$$

From (12)-(17) we obtain after rearranging the terms that [Insert (13), (14), (15), (16), and (17) into (12); collect all multiples of $\|x_n-p_n\|^2$ on the left and all multiples of $\|x_{n-1}-p_{n-1}\|^2$ on the right.]

$$
(f + h) (p _ {n}) + M _ {1, n} \| x _ {n} - p _ {n} \| ^ {2} \leq (f + h) (p _ {n - 1}) + M _ {2, n} \| x _ {n - 1} - p _ {n - 1} \| ^ {2}, \tag {18}
$$

where

$$
M _ {1, n} = \frac {\sigma}{2 \lambda_ {n}} - L _ {\nabla h} - \nu - \frac {\alpha_ {n}}{\lambda_ {n}} \mu
$$

and

$$
\begin{array}{l} M _ {2, n} = \lambda_ {n - 1} ^ {2} L _ {\nabla h} ^ {2} \left(\frac {L _ {\nabla h} ^ {2}}{2 \nu} + \nu + L _ {\nabla h} + \frac {L _ {\nabla u}}{2 \lambda_ {n}}\right) \\ + \frac {\alpha_ {n}}{\lambda_ {n}} \left(\mu \lambda_ {n - 1} ^ {2} L _ {\nabla h} ^ {2} + \frac {(1 + \lambda_ {n - 1} L _ {\nabla h}) ^ {2}}{2 \mu}\right). \\ \end{array}
$$ [Finally, $\lambda_n\le\overline\lambda$, $\lambda_n\ge\underline\lambda$, $0\le\alpha_n\le\alpha$, and $\lambda_{n-1}\le\overline\lambda$ imply $M_{1,n}\ge M_1$ and $M_{2,n}\le M_2$, so (18) implies (9).]

items.name: Lemma 3.3
Lemma 3.4
items.proof:
(iii) the sequence $((f + h)(p_n))_{n\geq 1}$ is convergent.

Proof From Lemma 3.2, we deduce that for every $n \geq 2$

$$
\begin{array}{l} (f + h) (p _ {n}) + M _ {2} \| x _ {n} - p _ {n} \| ^ {2} + (M _ {1} - M _ {2}) \| x _ {n} - p _ {n} \| ^ {2} \leq (f + h) (p _ {n - 1}) \\ + M _ {2} \| x _ {n - 1} - p _ {n - 1} \| ^ {2}. \tag {21} \\ \end{array}
$$ [Here $M_1-M_2>0$ by Lemma 3.3. Set $a_n=(f+h)(p_n)+M_2\|x_n-p_n\|^2$ and $b_n=(M_1-M_2)\|x_n-p_n\|^2$. Since $f+h$ is bounded from below and $M_2\|x_n-p_n\|^2\ge0$, the sequence $(a_n)$ is bounded below, and (21) has the form $a_n+b_n\le a_{n-1}$. Lemma 2.2 therefore gives convergence of $(a_n)$ and $\sum_{n\ge2}\|x_n-p_n\|^2<+\infty$. Relation (14) then gives $\sum_n\|x_{n+1}-x_n\|^2<+\infty$. Since $M_2\|x_n-p_n\|^2\to0$, convergence of $a_n$ implies convergence of $((f+h)(p_n))$.]

items.name: Lemma 3.5
items.statement:
The following lemma provides an estimate for some elements in the limiting sub-differential.

Lemma 3.5 In the setting of Problem 3.1, consider the sequences generated by Algorithm 3.1. Then, we have for every $n \geq 2$ :

$$
s _ {n} \in \partial (f + h) (p _ {n}), \tag {22}
$$

where

$$
\begin{array}{l} s _ {n} = \frac {1}{\lambda_ {n}} \big (\nabla u (x _ {n}) - \nabla u (p _ {n}) \big) + \nabla h (p _ {n}) - \nabla h (x _ {n}) + \frac {\alpha_ {n}}{\lambda_ {n}} (p _ {n - 1} - x _ {n - 1}) \\ + \frac {\alpha_ {n} \lambda_ {n - 1}}{\lambda_ {n}} \big (\nabla h (x _ {n - 1}) - \nabla h (p _ {n - 1}) \big). \\ \end{array}
$$

Moreover,
items.proof:
$$

Proof Take $n \geq 2$ . By using the formula for the subdifferential of the sum, from (4) it follows that

$$
0 \in \partial f (p _ {n}) + \frac {1}{\lambda_ {n}} \big (\nabla u (p _ {n}) - \nabla u (x _ {n}) \big) + \nabla h (x _ {n}) + \frac {\alpha_ {n}}{\lambda_ {n}} (x _ {n - 1} - x _ {n}),
$$

hence

$$
0 \in \partial (f + h) (p _ {n}) + \frac {1}{\lambda_ {n}} \big (\nabla u (p _ {n}) - \nabla u (x _ {n}) \big) + \nabla h (x _ {n}) - \nabla h (p _ {n}) + \frac {\alpha_ {n}}{\lambda_ {n}} (x _ {n - 1} - x _ {n}).
$$

Relation (22) follows from the above identity, by using also that [Move all explicit vector terms to the other side of the inclusion and rewrite $x_{n-1}-x_n$ via the second line of Algorithm 3.1 at index $n-1$; the resulting selected subgradient is exactly $s_n$.]

$$
\begin{array}{l} x _ {n - 1} - x _ {n} = x _ {n - 1} - p _ {n - 1} - (x _ {n} - p _ {n - 1}) = x _ {n - 1} - p _ {n - 1} \\ - \lambda_ {n - 1} \big (\nabla h (x _ {n - 1}) - \nabla h (p _ {n - 1}) \big). \\ \end{array}
$$ [For (23), apply the triangle inequality to the displayed formula for $s_n$, then use $\|\nabla u(x_n)-\nabla u(p_n)\|\le L_{\nabla u}\|x_n-p_n\|$ and $\|\nabla h(x_n)-\nabla h(p_n)\|\le L_{\nabla h}\|x_n-p_n\|$, together with $\|\nabla h(x_{n-1})-\nabla h(p_{n-1})\|\le L_{\nabla h}\|x_{n-1}-p_{n-1}\|$.]

items.name: Existence of minimizers for proper lsc coercive functions
items.statement: If $g:\mathbb{R}^m\to]-\infty,+\infty]$ is proper, lower semicontinuous, and coercive, then $\inf_{x\in\mathbb{R}^m}g(x)$ is finite and the infimum is attained.
items.proof: Cited from: Rockafellar, R.T., Wets, R.J.-B.: Variational Analysis, Fundamental Principles of Mathematical Sciences, vol. 317. Springer, Berlin (1998), cited as [30] in Lemma 3.6.

items.name: Cluster set properties under vanishing increments
items.statement: For a bounded sequence $(z_n)$ in a finite-dimensional Euclidean space with $z_{n+1}-z_n\to0$, the cluster set $\omega((z_n))$ is nonempty, compact, and connected, and $\operatorname{dist}(z_n,\omega((z_n)))\to0$.
items.proof: Cited from: Bolte, J., Sabach, S., Teboulle, M.: Proximal alternating linearized minimization for nonconvex and nonsmooth problems. Math. Program. Ser. A 146(1-2), 459-494 (2014), Lemma 5 and Remark 5, cited in Lemma 3.6.

items.name: Lemma 3.6
items.statement:
In the following, we use the notation $\omega((p_{n})_{n\geq1})$ for the set of cluster points of the sequence $(p_{n})_{n\geq1}$ . Next, we will give some properties of this set (see [20]).

Lemma 3.6 In the setting of Problem 3.1, suppose that the function $f + h$ is coercive (that is $\lim_{\| x \| \to +\infty}(f + h)(x) = +\infty$ ) and consider the sequences generated in Algorithm 3.1, where $\nu, \mu, \underline{\lambda}, \overline{\lambda}$ and $\alpha$ are chosen as in Lemma 3.3. Then, the following statements are true:

(i) $\emptyset \neq \omega((p_n)_{n\geq 1})\subseteq crit(f + h);$  
(ii) $\lim_{n\to +\infty}dist(p_n,\omega ((p_n)_{n\geq 1})) = 0;$
items.proof:
(iv) $f + h$ is finite and constant on $\omega((p_n)_{n\geq 1})$ .

Proof Since $f + h$ is a proper, lower semicontinuous and coercive function, it follows that $\inf_{x \in \mathbb{R}^m}[f(x) + h(x)]$ is finite and the infimum is attained (see [30]). Hence $f + h$ is bounded from below. [This is the direct method in finite dimension: coercivity confines a minimizing sequence to a bounded lower level set, lower semicontinuity gives a minimizer on its compact closure, and properness excludes the value $+\infty$ everywhere.]

(i) According to Lemma 3.4(ii), we have

$$
\begin{array}{l} (f + h) (p _ {n}) \leq (f + h) (p _ {n}) + M _ {2} \| x _ {n} - p _ {n} \| ^ {2} \leq (f + h) (p _ {1}) \\ + M _ {2} \| x _ {1} - p _ {1} \| ^ {2} \forall n \geq 1. \\ \end{array}
$$

Since the function $f + h$ is coercive, its lower level sets are bounded and we conclude that $(p_n)_{n > 1}$ is bounded, hence $\omega((p_n)_{n > 1}) \neq \emptyset$ . [The displayed uniform upper bound places every $p_n$ in one lower level set of the coercive function $f+h$; this lower level set is bounded, so Bolzano-Weierstrass gives a convergent subsequence.]

Take an arbitrary $p^* \in \omega((p_n)_{n \geq 1})$ . There exists a subsequence $(p_{n_k})_{k \in \mathbb{N}}$ such that $p_{n_k} \to p^*$ as $k \to +\infty$ . We show in the following that $\lim_{k \to +\infty} f(p_{n_k}) = f(p^*)$ . Notice that the lower semicontinuity of the function $f$ ensures $\liminf_{k \to +\infty} f(p_{n_k}) \geq f(p^*)$ . Moreover, from (4), we have that for every $n \geq 1$

$$
\begin{array}{l} f (p _ {n}) + \frac {1}{\lambda_ {n}} D _ {u} (p _ {n}, x _ {n}) + \langle p _ {n}, \nabla h (x _ {n}) \rangle + \frac {\alpha_ {n}}{\lambda_ {n}} \langle p _ {n}, x _ {n - 1} - x _ {n} \rangle \\ \leq f (p ^ {*}) + \frac {1}{\lambda_ {n}} D _ {u} (p ^ {*}, x _ {n}) + \left\langle p ^ {*}, \nabla h (x _ {n}) \right\rangle + \frac {\alpha_ {n}}{\lambda_ {n}} \left\langle p ^ {*}, x _ {n - 1} - x _ {n} \right\rangle . \\ \end{array}
$$

By using Lemma 3.4(i), (5) and by taking into consideration the bounds of the sequences involved, it follows $\limsup_{k\to +\infty}f(p_{n_k})\leq f(p^*)$ [Along the subsequence, Lemma 3.4(i) and (13)-(14) give $x_{n_k}-p_{n_k}\to0$ and $x_{n_k-1}-p_{n_k-1}\to0$; boundedness and continuity of $h,\nabla h,u,\nabla u$ make every extra term in the minimizer inequality converge to the corresponding term at $p^*$, leaving only the claimed upper bound for $f$.] , hence $\lim_{k\to +\infty}f(p_{n_k}) = f(p^*)$ .

Further, using Lemma 3.5, we have $s_{n_k} \in \partial(f + h)(p_{n_k})$ for all $k \geq 2$ . By using (23) and Lemma 3.4(i), from $p_{n_k} \to p^*$ it follows that $s_{n_k} \to 0$ as $k \to +\infty$ . Since we additionally have that $\lim_{k \to +\infty}(f + h)(p_{n_k}) = (f + h)(p^*)$ , the closedness of the graph of the limiting subdifferential operator guarantees that $0 \in \partial(f + h)(p^*)$ , thus $p^* \in \text{crit}(f + h)$ .

The proof of (ii) and (iii) can be done in the lines of [20, Lemma 5], by also taking into consideration [20, Remark 5], where it is noticed that the properties (ii) and (iii) are generic for sequences satisfying $p_{n+1} - p_n \to 0$ as $n \to +\infty$ . [Here $p_{n+1}-p_n=(p_{n+1}-x_{n+1})+(x_{n+1}-x_n)+(x_n-p_n)\to0$ by Lemma 3.4(i), so ext_thm_3 applies to $(p_n)$.]

items.name: Lemma 3.7
items.statement:
The following result characterizes the set of cluster points of the sequence $(p_n, x_n)_{n \geq 1}$ .

Lemma 3.7 In the setting of Problem 3.1, suppose that the function $f + h$ is coercive, consider the sequences generated in Algorithm 3.1, where $\nu, \mu, \underline{\lambda}, \overline{\lambda}$ and $\alpha$ are chosen as in Lemma 3.3, and the constants $M_1$ and $M_2$ as in Lemma 3.2. We introduce the function $H: \mathbb{R}^m \times \mathbb{R}^m \to \overline{\mathbb{R}}$ defined by

$$
H (x, y) = (f + h) (x) + M _ {2} \| x - y \| ^ {2} \forall (x, y) \in \mathbb {R} ^ {m} \times \mathbb {R} ^ {m}. \tag {24}
$$

Then, the following statements are true:

$$
(i) \emptyset \neq \omega ((p _ {n}, x _ {n}) _ {n \geq 1}) \subseteq c r i t (H) = \{(x, x) \in \mathbb {R} ^ {m} \times \mathbb {R} ^ {m}: x \in c r i t (f + h) \};
$$

(ii) $\lim_{n\to +\infty}dist((p_n,x_n),\omega ((p_n,x_n)_{n\geq 1})) = 0;$
items.proof:
(iv) $H$ is finite and constant on $\omega((p_n, x_n)_{n \geq 1})$ .

Proof The proof is similar to the one of Lemma 3.6 by noticing that for every $n \geq 2$ (see (21)) [Apply Lemma 3.6 to the product sequence $z_n=(p_n,x_n)$. Lemma 3.4(i) gives $z_{n+1}-z_n\to0$, and boundedness follows from boundedness of $(p_n)$ plus $x_n-p_n\to0$.]

$$
H (p _ {n}, x _ {n}) + (M _ {1} - M _ {2}) \| x _ {n} - p _ {n} \| ^ {2} \leq H (p _ {n - 1}, x _ {n - 1}) \tag {25}
$$

and

$$
(s _ {n} + 2 M _ {2} (p _ {n} - x _ {n}), 2 M _ {2} (x _ {n} - p _ {n})) \in \partial H (p _ {n}, x _ {n}), \tag {26}
$$

where $(s_n)_{n\geq 2}$ is the sequence introduced in Lemma 3.5. Relation (26) follows from
$$ [For all $(x,y)$, the smooth part $M_2\|x-y\|^2$ has gradient $(2M_2(x-y),2M_2(y-x))$, hence by the subdifferential sum rule
$$
\partial H(x,y)=\big(\partial(f+h)(x)+2M_2(x-y)\big)\times\{2M_2(y-x)\}.
$$
Using $s_n\in\partial(f+h)(p_n)$ from Lemma 3.5 gives (26). The remaining assertions follow as in Lemma 3.6, with ext_thm_3 giving distance-to-cluster-set convergence, compactness, and connectedness.]

items.name: Theorem 3.1
items.statement:
We are now in position to prove the convergence of the Tseng's type algorithm provided that $H$ is a KL function.

Theorem 3.1 In the setting of Problem 3.1, suppose that the function $f + h$ is coercive, consider the sequences generated in Algorithm 3.1, where $\nu, \mu, \underline{\lambda}, \overline{\lambda}$ and $\alpha$ are chosen as in Lemma 3.3, and the constants $M_1$ and $M_2$ as in Lemma 3.2. We assume that

$$
H: \mathbb {R} ^ {m} \times \mathbb {R} ^ {m} \to \overline {{\mathbb {R}}}, H (x, y) = (f + h) (x) + M _ {2} \| x - y \| ^ {2} \forall (x, y) \in \mathbb {R} ^ {m} \times \mathbb {R} ^ {m},
$$

is a KL function. Then, the following statements are true:
items.proof:
(ii) there exists $x \in \text{crit}(f + h)$ such that $\lim_{n \to +\infty} x_n = \lim_{n \to +\infty} p_n = x$ .

Proof (i) According to Lemma 3.7(i), we can consider an element $p^* \in \operatorname{crit}(f + h)$ such that $(p^*, p^*) \in \omega((p_n, x_n)_{n \geq 1})$ . In analogy to the proof of Lemma 3.6 one can easily show that $\lim_{n \to +\infty} H(p_n, x_n) = H(p^*, p^*)$ . [Indeed, (25) and $M_1>M_2$ make $H(p_n,x_n)$ decreasing and convergent; along a subsequence converging to $(p^*,p^*)$, Lemma 3.7(iv) identifies the subsequential limit with $H(p^*,p^*)$.] We consider two cases.

I. There exists $\overline{n} \in \mathbb{N}$ such that $H(p_{\overline{n}}, x_{\overline{n}}) = H(p^*, p^*)$ . The decrease property in (25) implies $H(p_n, x_n) = H(p^*, p^*)$ for every $n \geq \overline{n}$ . One can show inductively that the sequence $(p_n, x_n)_{n \geq \overline{n}}$ is constant and the conclusion follows. [Since (25) has a nonnegative decrease term, equality of the endpoint values forces $\|x_n-p_n\|=0$ for all $n\ge\overline n+1$; then (4) gives $x_{n+1}=p_n=x_n$, and the argmin step repeats the same point.]  
II. For all $n \geq 1$ we have $H(p_n, x_n) > H(p^*, p^*)$ . Take $\Omega := \omega((p_n, x_n)_{n \geq 1})$ . Since $H$ is a KL function, from Lemma 3.7(iii)-(iv) and Lemma 2.1, there exist $\varepsilon, \eta > 0$ and $\varphi \in \Theta_\eta$ such that for all $(x, y)$ in the intersection

$$
\begin{array}{l} \{(x, y) \in \mathbb {R} ^ {m} \times \mathbb {R} ^ {m}: \mathrm{dist} ((x, y), \Omega) <   \varepsilon \} \\ \cap \{(x, y) \in \mathbb {R} ^ {m} \times \mathbb {R} ^ {m}: H (p ^ {*}, p ^ {*}) <   H (x, y) <   H (p ^ {*}, p ^ {*}) + \eta \} \tag {27} \\ \end{array}
$$

the following inequality holds

$$
\varphi^ {\prime} (H (x, y) - H (p ^ {*}, p ^ {*})) \mathrm{dist} ((0, 0), \partial H (x, y)) \geq 1. \tag {28}
$$

Let be $n_1 \geq 1$ such that $H(p_n, x_n) < H(p^*, p^*) + \eta$ for every $n \geq n_1$ . Moreover, from Lemma 3.7(ii), there exists $n_2 \in \mathbb{N}$ such that $\text{dist}((p_n, x_n), \Omega) < \varepsilon$ for every $n \geq n_2$ . Thus, the sequence $(p_n, x_n)_{n \geq N}$ belongs to the intersection in (27), where $N = \max\{n_1, n_2\}$ . From (28), we have

$$
\varphi^ {\prime} (H (p _ {n}, x _ {n}) - H (p ^ {*}, p ^ {*})) \mathrm{dist} ((0, 0), \partial H (p _ {n}, x _ {n})) \geq 1 \forall n \geq N. \tag {29}
$$

Further, since $\varphi$ is a concave function, we get for every $n \geq 1$ the following inequality:

$$
\begin{array}{l} \varphi \Big (H (p _ {n}, x _ {n}) - H (p ^ {*}, p ^ {*}) \Big) - \varphi \Big (H (p _ {n + 1}, x _ {n + 1}) - H (p ^ {*}, p ^ {*}) \Big) \\ \geq \varphi^ {\prime} \Big (H (p _ {n}, x _ {n}) - H (p ^ {*}, p ^ {*}) \Big) \cdot \Big (H (p _ {n}, x _ {n}) - H (p _ {n + 1}, x _ {n + 1}) \Big). \tag {30} \\ \end{array}
$$

Moreover, from (29) and (26) we have

$$
\varphi^ {\prime} \Big (H (p _ {n}, x _ {n}) - H (p ^ {*}, p ^ {*}) \Big) \geq \frac {1}{\| (s _ {n} + 2 M _ {2} (p _ {n} - x _ {n}) , 2 M _ {2} (x _ {n} - p _ {n})) \|} \forall n \geq N. \tag {31}
$$

By using for every $n \geq 1$ the notation

$$
\Delta_ {n, n + 1} := \varphi \big (H (p _ {n}, x _ {n}) - H (p ^ {*}, p ^ {*}) \big) - \varphi \big (H (p _ {n + 1}, x _ {n + 1}) - H (p ^ {*}, p ^ {*}) \big),
$$

from (30), (31) and (25) we deduce

$$
\Delta_ {n, n + 1} \geq (M _ {1} - M _ {2}) \cdot \frac {\| x _ {n + 1} - p _ {n + 1} \| ^ {2}}{\sqrt {\| s _ {n} + 2 M _ {2} (p _ {n} - x _ {n}) \| ^ {2} + 4 M _ {2} ^ {2} \| x _ {n} - p _ {n} \| ^ {2}}} \forall n \geq N. \tag {32}
$$

From here we obtain [Apply $2ab\le a^2+b^2$ in the form $r\le (\delta/2)A+r^2/(2\delta A)$ to (32), with $r=\|x_{n+1}-p_{n+1}\|$ and $A$ equal to the denominator in (32); this yields (33) after solving for $r$.]

$$
\begin{array}{l} \| x _ {n + 1} - p _ {n + 1} \| \leq \frac {\delta}{2} \sqrt {\| s _ {n} + 2 M _ {2} (p _ {n} - x _ {n}) \| ^ {2} + 4 M _ {2} ^ {2} \| x _ {n} - p _ {n} \| ^ {2}} \\ + \frac {\Delta_ {n , n + 1}}{2 \delta (M _ {1} - M _ {2})} \forall n \geq N, \tag {33} \\ \end{array}
$$

where $\delta > 0$ is chosen such that the following inequality holds:

$$
\frac {\delta \sqrt {2}}{2} \left(\sqrt {\left(\frac {L _ {\nabla u}}{\underline {{\lambda}}} + L _ {\nabla h} + 2 M _ {2}\right) ^ {2} + 4 M _ {2} ^ {2}} + \frac {\alpha}{\underline {{\lambda}}} (1 + \bar {\lambda} L _ {\nabla h})\right) <   1. \tag {34}
$$

Moreover, we have for every $n \geq 1$ (see (23))

$$
\begin{array}{l} \sqrt {\| s _ {n} + 2 M _ {2} (p _ {n} - x _ {n}) \| ^ {2} + 4 M _ {2} ^ {2} \| x _ {n} - p _ {n} \| ^ {2}} \\ \leq \sqrt {\left[ 2 \left(\frac {L _ {\nabla u}}{\lambda_ {n}} + L _ {\nabla h} + 2 M _ {2}\right) ^ {2} + 4 M _ {2} ^ {2} \right] \| x _ {n} - p _ {n} \| ^ {2} + 2 \frac {\alpha_ {n} ^ {2}}{\lambda_ {n} ^ {2}} \left(1 + \lambda_ {n - 1} L _ {\nabla h}\right) ^ {2} \| x _ {n - 1} - p _ {n - 1} \| ^ {2}} \\ \leq \sqrt \left[ 2 \left(\frac {L _ {\nabla u}}{\lambda_ {n}} + L _ {\nabla h} + 2 M _ {2}\right) ^ {2} + 4 M _ {2} ^ {2} \right] \| x _ {n} - p _ {n} \| + \sqrt {2} \frac {\alpha_ {n}}{\lambda_ {n}} \left(1 + \lambda_ {n - 1} L _ {\nabla h}\right) \| x _ {n - 1} - p _ {n - 1} \| \\ \leq \sqrt {\left[ 2 \left(\frac {L _ {\nabla u}}{\underline {{\lambda}}} + L _ {\nabla h} + 2 M _ {2}\right) ^ {2} + 4 M _ {2} ^ {2} \right] \| x _ {n} - p _ {n} \| + \sqrt {2} \frac {\alpha}{\underline {{\lambda}}} \left(1 + \bar {\lambda} L _ {\nabla h}\right) \| x _ {n - 1} - p _ {n - 1} \|.} \\ \end{array}
$$

We derive from (33) that [Insert the previous bound on the square-root term, then absorb the uniform constants into the definitions of $a$ and $b$. The choice (34) makes $a+b<1$.]

$$
\| x _ {n + 1} - p _ {n + 1} \| \leq a \| x _ {n} - p _ {n} \| + b \| x _ {n - 1} - p _ {n - 1} \| + \frac {\Delta_ {n , n + 1}}{2 \delta (M _ {1} - M _ {2})} \forall n \geq N, \tag {35}
$$

where

$$
a := \frac {\delta \sqrt {2}}{2} \left(\sqrt {\left(\frac {L _ {\nabla u}}{\underline {{\lambda}}} + L _ {\nabla h} + 2 M _ {2}\right) ^ {2} + 4 M _ {2} ^ {2}}\right) \text {and} b := \frac {\delta \sqrt {2}}{2} \frac {\alpha}{\underline {{\lambda}}} \left(1 + \overline {{\lambda}} L _ {\nabla h}\right).
$$

Notice that due to (34) we have $a + b < 1$ . Now, for a fixed $k \geq 1$ we have (since $\varphi$ takes only non-negative values)

$$
\begin{array}{l} \sum_ {n = 1} ^ {k} \Delta_ {n, n + 1} = \varphi \big (H (p _ {1}, x _ {1}) - H (p ^ {*}, p ^ {*}) \big) - \varphi \big (H (p _ {k + 1}, x _ {k + 1}) - H (p ^ {*}, p ^ {*}) \big) \\ \leq \varphi \big (H (p _ {1}, x _ {1}) - H (p ^ {*}, p ^ {*}) \big), \\ \end{array}
$$

hence

$$
\sum_ {n \geq 1} \frac {\Delta_ {n , n + 1}}{2 \delta (M _ {1} - M _ {2})} <   + \infty .
$$

From (35) and Lemma 2.3 we conclude that $\sum_{n\geq 1}\| x_n - p_n\| < +\infty$ . [Use Lemma 2.3 with $\xi_n=\|x_n-p_n\|$ and $\varepsilon_n=\Delta_{n,n+1}/(2\delta(M_1-M_2))$, whose summability was just proved.] Further, from (14), we obtain $\sum_{n\in \mathbb{N}}\| x_{n + 1} - x_n\| < +\infty$ . [For the proof of (ii), (i) gives $\sum_n\|x_{n+1}-x_n\|<+\infty$, so $(x_n)$ is Cauchy in $\mathbb R^m$ and converges to some $x$; also $\|x_n-p_n\|\to0$, hence $p_n\to x$. Lemma 3.7(i) then gives $(x,x)\in\operatorname{crit}(H)$ and therefore $x\in\operatorname{crit}(f+h)$.]

items.name: Semi-algebraic functions are KL and stable under finite sums
items.statement: Semi-algebraic extended-real-valued functions are KL functions, and the class of semi-algebraic functions is stable under finite sums; hence if $f+h$ is semi-algebraic, then $H(x,y)=(f+h)(x)+M_2\|x-y\|^2$ is a KL function.
items.proof: Cited from: Bolte, J., Sabach, S., Teboulle, M.: Proximal alternating linearized minimization for nonconvex and nonsmooth problems. Math. Program. Ser. A 146(1-2), 459-494 (2014), cited in Corollary 3.1 and in the KL background discussion.

items.name: Corollary 3.1
items.statement:
The following corollary is a direct consequence of Theorem 3.1.

Corollary 3.1 In the setting of Problem 3.1, suppose that the function $f + h$ is coercive and semi-algebraic, consider the sequences generated in Algorithm 3.1, where $\nu, \mu, \underline{\lambda}, \overline{\lambda}$ and $\alpha$ are chosen as in Lemma 3.3. Then, the following statements are true:
items.proof: (ii) there exists $x \in \text{crit}(f + h)$ such that $\lim_{n \to +\infty} x_n = \lim_{n \to +\infty} p_n = x$ . [By ext_thm_4, semi-algebraicity of $f+h$ and of $(x,y)\mapsto M_2\|x-y\|^2$ implies that $H$ is semi-algebraic and hence a KL function, which is exactly the additional hypothesis of Theorem 3.1.]
